"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"Cost is concentrated in the closed-loop stage: 150 rollouts x 135 features = 20,250 sequential 300-step episodes, each gated by a 150 ms VLA forward pass. This budget is spent uniformly on every feature, including the majority that do nothing, and rollouts are already independent so raw GPU count only buys the ~2x batching that RLinf-VLA demonstrated.\",\"assumption\":\"A feature's value can only be judged by closed-loop task success, so every candidate feature must pay the full 150-rollout price before anything is known about it.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the order of steps: screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size. Compute then buys feature coverage instead of redundant rollouts.\",\"question\":\"On one LIBERO task with pi0.5, what is the Spearman rank correlation between per-feature open-loop steered-vs-unsteered action divergence (L2 on action tokens over a fixed observation buffer) and per-feature closed-loop success-rate delta across 10 features spanning the divergence range?\",\"measure\":\"Record ~200 unsteered episodes and their activations on one task (a few GPU-hours), apply each of the 135 steering vectors open-loop to get divergence scores (~1 A100-day, ~$25), then run 25 closed-loop rollouts for each of 10 chosen features in a batched simulator (~1 A100-day). Compute the rank correlation. No real robot needed.\",\"compute_after\":\"If the correlation holds, the same compute screens 10-100x more features per study, or the 135-feature sweep shrinks ~10x in cost, freeing budget to sweep features on contact-rich simulated tasks that currently get no coverage.\",\"exact\":\"Spearman rho between per-feature mean open-loop action divergence and per-feature closed-loop success delta, over 10 features, plus the recall of truly-effective features in the open-loop top-20.\",\"expected\":\"Rho >= 0.7 and top-20 recall >= 0.8 would make screening the default; even rho ~ 0.4 with a cheap top-20 cutoff cuts cost roughly 5x.\",\"fails_if\":\"Open-loop divergence does not predict closed-loop effect (compounding errors, features that only matter under contact and never fire on the recorded buffer), or all divergences are near zero so the ranking is noise.\",\"closest_prior\":\"The 420,000-rollout / 520-SAE sweep (arXiv 2603.19233) pays full closed-loop cost per feature; open-loop action-divergence is the standard cheap proxy in LLM activation-steering evals but is unpublished for VLAs.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"The binary success metric forces ~150 rollouts per condition to resolve an effect and yields one bit per episode; it also cannot ask whether steering controls any contact variable without a full validated cloth task, which simulation cannot currently provide.\",\"assumption\":\"The unit of evidence is task-level success on a rigid pick-and-place benchmark, so effects smaller than a success-rate swing, and any control of contact rather than motion, are invisible.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured: replace binary success with a continuous physical readout (wrist force/torque trace, contact timing, peak grasp force) on a short instrumented real-robot task such as grasping a compliant object, and regress steering strength against the readout so each trial yields a slope. This tests control of contact behaviour directly and sidesteps the unvalidated cloth simulator.\",\"question\":\"On a real pi0.5-class arm grasping a deformable object with a wrist force/torque sensor, does any of ~10 candidate SAE or FFN steering directions produce a monotone change in peak grasp force (newtons) across 5 steering strengths, versus sham random directions?\",\"measure\":\"10 directions x 5 strengths x 5 repeats = 250 real grasps, roughly 1-2 robot-days (~$2-5k) plus trivial GPU time; fit slope per direction and compare against the null distribution from random directions. Cheapest kill-criterion: if even the strongest known steering feature shows no force-trace effect in 25 trials, stop.\",\"compute_after\":\"If slopes exist, a handful of real trials validates each candidate, so compute shifts to wide sim-screened sweeps with cheap real confirmation (~25 trials per candidate instead of 150), a ~30x reduction in the expensive stage; if no slope exists, the cloth/deformable steering question is dead regardless of compute.\",\"exact\":\"Slope in newtons per unit steering coefficient and its t-statistic per direction, against the null distribution from random directions, plus minimum detectable effect at 25 trials.\",\"expected\":\"Given Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot), at least one direction should shift applied force or contact timing measurably within 25 trials.\",\"fails_if\":\"No direction moves the force trace beyond trial-to-trial noise, meaning steering modulates high-level plans but not contact execution, so no sweep size can reveal cloth control that is not there.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Grant et al. motor-program binding on UR10e; COAST conceptors reporting +40% on three real tasks with binary metrics only; Goodfire marketing steering for robotics with no published numbers.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"For cloth and dish-rack tasks the binding constraint is not throughput but validity: steering effects measured in simulation are asserted not to transfer for deformables, so every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same rigid-task evidence and nothing about the actual blocker.\",\"assumption\":\"The answer needed is 'which features control cloth behaviour', which presumes a trustworthy cloth simulator; without one, sim compute is uninformative and the sim-vs-real transfer of steering effects has never been measured even where it could be.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective: before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function of steering effect sizes on rigid tasks where both sides are cheap. If per-intervention effect direction and magnitude correlate between a GPU-parallel simulator and the real robot, simulation becomes a validated screening instrument; independently, measure whether the simulator predicts force traces for compliant objects, which is the fidelity threshold cloth screening would require.\",\"question\":\"Across >= 10 steering interventions on rigid DROID-style tasks, what is the sign agreement and rank correlation between each intervention's success-rate delta in a batched simulator (200 rollouts) and on the real robot (25 trials)?\",\"measure\":\"10 interventions x 200 batched sim rollouts (~1 A100-day, ~$25) + 10 x 25 real trials (~1-2 robot-days, ~$2-5k). Report sign agreement and Spearman rho of the deltas. Separately, log sim-vs-real wrist force traces on one compliant grasp and report trace error.\",\"compute_after\":\"If sign agreement >= 9/10 and rho >= 0.8, every GPU-dollar afterward buys validated screening and the field can cheaply sweep deformable-adjacent proxies; if agreement is poor, all sim spending on steering should stop and compute should be redirected to real-robot parallelization (many arms, many objects) instead.\",\"exact\":\"Sign-agreement rate and Spearman rho of per-intervention sim vs real success deltas, plus sim-vs-real force-trace RMSE on the compliant-grasp probe.\",\"expected\":\"Rigid-task transfer plausibly holds (consistent with sim benchmarks and RLinf-VLA throughput results) but is unmeasured for steering; the force-trace probe on a compliant object is expected to show a clear gap, quantifying exactly how far sim is from supporting cloth claims.\",\"fails_if\":\"Even 2-3 of 10 rigid interventions flip sign between sim and real, showing sim sweeps are noise for steering specifically, in which case more GPU compute only buys faster wrong answers.\",\"closest_prior\":\"RLinf-VLA (1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments) establishes the throughput side but not effect transfer; no published sim-vs-real correlation of steering effect sizes exists; the 420k-rollout sweep (arXiv 2603.19233) is entirely rigid-task and does not test transfer.\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"items\"],\"properties\":{\"items\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"index\",\"kind\",\"meets_criterion\",\"quote\",\"reason\"],\"properties\":{\"index\":{\"type\":\"integer\"},\"kind\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"reframe\",\"copies\",\"other\"]},\"meets_criterion\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"yes\",\"no\",\"NA\"]},\"quote\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reason\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me analyze each proposal.

Criterion: "The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."

This is essentially: does the proposal use open-loop screening on fixed recorded observations, then confirm top candidates with closed-loop episodes?

Proposal 1:
- Reframe: "screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size."
- Question: Spearman correlation between per-feature open-loop steered-vs-unsteered action divergence on fixed observation buffer and closed-loop success delta across 10 features. Then run 25 closed-loop rollouts for each of 10 chosen features.
- This matches the criterion exactly: open-loop scoring on fixed recorded observations, confirming top candidates with closed-loop episodes. meets_criterion: yes.
- Kind: It changes what is computed/measured (open-loop divergence instead of closed-loop success for screening) so more compute buys feature coverage instead of redundant rollouts. This is a reframe. kind: "reframe".

Proposal 2:
- Reframe: "Change what is measured: replace binary success with a continuous physical readout (wrist force/torque trace, contact timing, peak grasp force) on a short instrumented real-robot task... and regress steering strength against the readout so each trial yields a slope."
- Question: On a real arm grasping a deformable object, does any of ~10 candidate steering directions produce monotone change in peak grasp force across 5 steering strengths vs sham random directions?
- This is real-robot closed-loop grasping (real trials on a real robot grasping an object — it's a physical closed loop, though the measure is continuous). It does not score on fixed recorded observations; it uses real robot trials. So meets_criterion: no — it doesn't use open-loop scoring on recorded observations. Actually, the criterion requires: "it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes." Proposal 2 uses full closed-loop real-robot trials (grasping), just with a continuous metric instead of binary success. So meets_criterion: no.
- Kind: It changes what is measured — continuous force readout instead of binary success, so each trial yields a slope rather than one bit. More compute buys more sensitivity per trial (each trial yields a slope). This changes what is measured so that more compute (trials) buys something it did not before — detection of effects smaller than success-rate swings, contact control. Hmm, is this "reframe"? The definition: "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before." Proposal 2 changes what is measured (continuous readout instead of binary success). So more compute (trials) buys detection of contact control that binary success couldn't reveal. Yes, this is a reframe.

But wait — does more compute buy something new? With continuous readout, each trial yields slope info; more trials give statistical power to detect smaller effects and regress against steering strength. Previously more rollouts only bought tighter success-rate estimates. So yes, reframe.

Proposal 3:
- Reframe: "Change the objective: before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function of steering effect sizes on rigid tasks where both sides are cheap... simulation becomes a validated screening instrument."
- Question: Across >= 10 steering interventions on rigid tasks, what is the sign agreement and rank correlation between each intervention's success-rate delta in a batched simulator (200 rollouts) and on the real robot (25 trials)?
- This is a validation/calibration study. It still runs closed-loop episodes (both sim and real). It doesn't score on fixed recorded observations. So meets_criterion: no.
- Kind: It changes what is measured/ordered? It changes the objective — measuring sim-vs-real transfer rather than steering effects themselves. Does more compute buy something it did not before? The proposal itself says: "every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same rigid-task evidence and nothing about the actual blocker" — so the reframe is to first measure transfer. But the question is about calibration, not about scaling compute. Hmm.

The kind classification: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise.

Proposal 3 changes what is computed/measured: instead of measuring steering effect sizes (success-rate deltas on tasks), it measures the correlation between sim and real deltas — i.e., the transfer function. If correlation holds, then sim compute becomes validated screening (buying something new: deformable-adjacent proxy sweeps). So more compute afterward buys validated screening. But the question itself is a calibration study — is it a reframe? The reframe changes the objective: measure transfer before sweeping. This changes what is measured so that subsequent compute buys something new (validated screening). I'd classify it as "reframe" — it changes what is computed/ordered (calibrate transfer first, then sweep) so that more compute buys validated screening rather than unvalidated evidence.

Alternatively, one might argue it's "other" — a validity study that doesn't change what compute buys directly; it's a gatekeeper. Hmm. But the criterion says "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before." The proposal explicitly says: "If per-intervention effect direction and magnitude correlate between a GPU-parallel simulator and the real robot, simulation becomes a validated screening instrument" and "If sign agreement >= 9/10 and rho >= 0.8, every GPU-dollar afterward buys validated screening." So more compute buys something new (validated screening). This is a reframe of the objective — measure transfer first. I'll say "reframe".

Actually, let me reconsider. The question itself measures sim-vs-real correlation using closed-loop rollouts on both sides. It doesn't itself buy more via compute — it's a calibration. But the classification is about the reframing behind the question: "Change the objective: before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function." This changes what is computed (transfer function instead of feature sweeps) so that more compute afterward buys validated screening. I think "reframe" is right.

Hmm, but could it be "other"? The reframe is about validity, not about making compute buy more. The proposal's bottleneck says: "the binding constraint is not throughput but validity: steering effects measured in simulation are asserted not to transfer for deformables, so every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same rigid-task evidence and nothing about the actual blocker." The reframe addresses this by measuring transfer. The effect: if transfer holds, compute buys validated screening (something new); if not, compute redirected. So the reframing does change what more compute buys. I'll go with "reframe".

Now let me double-check proposal 1's meets_criterion: "The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."

Proposal 1: "screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size." Measure: "apply each of the 135 steering vectors open-loop to get divergence scores... then run 25 closed-loop rollouts for each of 10 chosen features."

Yes, exactly: open-loop scoring on fixed recorded observations buffer, closed-loop confirmation only for top candidates (10 chosen features). meets_criterion: yes.

The criterion says "confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes" — proposal 1 runs closed-loop for 10 chosen features (top-k by effect size). Yes.

Proposal 2: Uses real-robot grasping trials with continuous force readout — this is closed-loop (real robot interacting with environment). It doesn't use fixed recorded observations. So no. Actually wait — is a real-robot grasp a "closed-loop episode"? The criterion is about removing the closed-loop dependency by scoring on fixed recorded observations. Proposal 2 does not do that; it changes the metric (continuous vs binary) but still runs full episodes (grasps). So meets_criterion: no.

Proposal 3: Runs closed-loop rollouts in sim and real trials; no fixed-observation open-loop scoring. meets_criterion: no.

Now, one nuance: could proposal 2's criterion be "NA"? The criterion is specific: removes closed-loop dependency via open-loop scoring on recorded observations. Proposal 2 clearly does not do this — it's a full closed-loop real-robot protocol. "no" is appropriate, not NA. NA might be used if the criterion doesn't apply, but here it applies (closed-loop is present) and is not removed. So "no".

For proposal 3, also "no".

Now quotes:
- Proposal 1 quote: "screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size"
- Proposal 2 quote: "replace binary success with a continuous physical readout (wrist force/torque trace, contact timing, peak grasp force) on a short instrumented real-robot task"
- Proposal 3 quote: "before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function of steering effect sizes on rigid tasks where both sides are cheap"

Reasons (max 25 words each):
1: "Screens all features on a fixed recorded-observation buffer open-loop, reserving closed-loop rollouts for top-k features only." — that's about 16 words. Good.
2: "Still runs full closed-loop real-robot grasp episodes; it swaps the metric to continuous force traces, not fixed-observation open-loop scoring." Good.
3: "Measures sim-vs-real transfer using closed-loop sim rollouts and real trials; no open-loop fixed-observation screening, no top-candidate confirmation structure." Count: Measures(1) sim-vs-real(2) transfer(3) using(4) closed-loop(5) sim(6) rollouts(7) and(8) real(9) trials(10) no(11) open-loop(12) fixed-observation(13) screening(14) no(15) top-candidate(16) confirmation(17) structure(18). 18 words. Good.

Kind reasons (should be in the reason field too? The schema has one reason per item. I need to combine kind justification and meets_criterion justification in one reason of at most 25 words. Hmm, that's tight. Let me look at the schema: items have index, kind, meets_criterion, quote, reason. One reason field. So the reason should justify both classifications? Or primarily the classification. I'll craft reasons that address kind primarily, maybe touching criterion.

Let me write reasons that cover both briefly:

1: kind=reframe, meets=yes. Reason: "Changes screening from closed-loop success to open-loop divergence on recorded observations; compute buys feature coverage, confirming only top candidates closed-loop." Count: Changes(1) screening(2) from(3) closed-loop(4) success(5) to(6) open-loop(7) divergence(8) on(9) recorded(10) observations(11) compute(12) buys(13) feature(14) coverage(15) confirming(16) only(17) top(18) candidates(19) closed-loop(20). 20 words. Good.

2: kind=reframe, meets=no. Reason: "Changes measurement from binary success to continuous force slopes, so extra trials buy contact-level evidence; but episodes remain fully closed-loop real grasps." Count: Changes(1) measurement(2) from(3) binary(4) success(5) to(6) continuous(7) force(8) slopes(9) so(10) extra(11) trials(12) buy(13) contact-level(14) evidence(15) but(16) episodes(17) remain(18) fully(19) closed-loop(20) real(21) grasps(22). 22 words. Good.

3: kind=reframe, meets=no. Reason: "Changes objective to calibrating sim-real transfer first, so later compute buys validated screening; question itself runs closed-loop sim rollouts and real trials." Count: Changes(1) objective(2) to(3) calibrating(4) sim-real(5) transfer(6) first(7) so(8) later(9) compute(10) buys(11) validated(12) screening(13) question(14) itself(15) runs(16) closed-loop(17) sim(18) rollouts(19) and(20) real(21) trials(22). 22 words. Good.

Hmm, for proposal 3, is "reframe" the right kind? Let me reconsider. The question measures sign agreement and rank correlation between sim and real success-rate deltas. This is a new computation (correlation of effect sizes across two platforms) rather than more rollouts of the same kind. And the reframe's stated purpose: "If ... correlate ..., simulation becomes a validated screening instrument" — i.e., after validation, compute buys something new. The proposal says "Change the objective". I think "reframe" fits: it changes what is computed/measured (transfer function vs effect sweeps) so that more compute buys something it did not before (validated screening, or a stop signal).

Alternatively, one could argue it's "other" because it's a validity/calibration question that gates compute rather than changing what compute buys. But the reframe explicitly reorders: "before sweeping anything new, calibrate..." — changing the order of steps so that subsequent compute buys validity. Hmm. The kind definition: "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". Proposal 3 changes the order (calibrate before sweeping) and what is measured (transfer function). And the compute_after says: "If sign agreement >= 9/10 and rho >= 0.8, every GPU-dollar afterward buys validated screening and the field can cheaply sweep deformable-adjacent proxies; if agreement is poor, all sim spending on steering should stop..." So more compute buys validated screening — something it did not before (unvalidated evidence). I'll go with "reframe".

Actually wait, let me think more carefully. Is it possible the intended answer for proposal 3 is "other"? The question is a calibration question — measuring transfer. It doesn't itself scale with compute to buy more; it's a fixed-size validation. But the criterion for "reframe" is about the reframing behind the question: does the reframe change what is computed/measured/ordered so that more compute buys something new? Proposal 3's reframe does exactly that — it changes the order (calibrate first) so that subsequent compute buys validated screening rather than unvalidated rigid evidence. The bottleneck statement: "every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same rigid-task evidence and nothing about the actual blocker" — the reframe fixes this. So yes, reframe.

Hmm, but one could also argue: the reframe doesn't make compute buy anything new; it just determines whether compute is useful at all. If transfer holds, compute buys what it already bought (screening) but now validated. Validation is new — before, sim evidence was unvalidated for steering. So sim compute would buy validated screening, which is genuinely new (it would unlock deformable-adjacent proxy sweeps). I'll stick with "reframe".

Let me reconsider proposal 2's kind too. "Change what is measured: replace binary success with a continuous physical readout... and regress steering strength against the readout so each trial yields a slope." More trials/compute now buy slope estimation and detection of contact effects that binary success couldn't see. This changes what is measured so more compute buys something new (contact-level evidence, sensitivity). Yes, reframe.

But wait — could proposal 2 be "other"? It's a real-robot experiment; more robot-days buy more trials. The change: continuous metric per trial, regression across strengths. Before, 150 rollouts bought one bit per episode resolving a success swing. After, each trial contributes to a slope, detecting smaller effects. So compute (trials) buys something it did not before — finer-grained contact evidence. That fits "reframe": changes what is measured so that more compute buys something it did not before. Yes.

Alternatively one might say the trials are still the same closed-loop grasps just repeated with a different sensor — "copies"? No — the measurement is different (force traces vs binary success), and the analysis is different (slopes). It's not just running the same computation more times. It's reframe.

For proposal 1: clearly reframe — reorder steps, screen open-loop first.

Now meets_criterion for each:

1: yes. Exactly matches: open-loop scoring on fixed recorded observations, confirm only top candidates (10 features) with closed-loop episodes.

2: no. Real-robot closed-loop grasps; no open-loop recorded-observation scoring.

3: no. Closed-loop sim rollouts + real trials; no open-loop recorded-observation screening.

Could any be "NA"? NA might be for cases where the criterion is inapplicable. But the schema allows "yes"/"no"/"NA". Here all are applicable in the sense that we can determine yes/no. I'll use yes/no.

Now quotes — should be from the proposal text. Let me pick representative quotes:

1: From reframe: "screen all features open-loop first by steering and measuring divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations, then pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k features by effect size"

2: From reframe: "replace binary success with a continuous physical readout (wrist force/torque trace, contact timing, peak grasp force) on a short instrumented real-robot task such as grasping a compliant object"

3: From reframe: "before sweeping anything new, calibrate the sim-to-real transfer function of steering effect sizes on rigid tasks where both sides are cheap"

These quotes support both kind and criterion judgments.

I'm fairly confident. One more consideration on proposal 3's kind — could it be "other"? The question measures sim-vs-real correlation; it doesn't scale with compute to buy more of anything; it's a gate. But the kind criterion says "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before".
